newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan fails to roil bullish US debt buy-siders.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan fails to roil bullish US debt buy-siders.

text.p: The buy side of the U.S. Treasury market has not been disturbed by the mammoth selloff that scared many players this week after hawkish comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Instead, optimistic-sounding U.S. money managers said the selling, which pushed long bond yields to 6.79 percent from 6.65 percent, created a solid buying opportunity.
"(Greenspan's) comments actually created more of a buying opportunity with regard to U.S. fixed-income," said Claude Erb, director of research First Chicago Investment Management Co

In the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins congressional testimony on Wednesday, Greenspan said he sees upside inflation risks. He added he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening of monetary policy to ward off any possible upsurge in inflation.
But U.S. money managers just do not seem to believe inflation will wake up and haunt the market any time soon.
"I'm still very optimistic on the bond market. I think the fundamentals are very good," said David Goldman, president of money management firm S.G. Capital Management.
"The fact is there's no inflation ... So I think we're going to see the long bond (yield) by 6.25 percent by the end of the year," Goldman added.

Goldman said he believes the market "overreacted" to the Fed chairman's comments. "Greenspan always speaks of the possibility of ... raising rates pre-emptively. This is a standard formula and there is nothing new," he said.
Analysts said they did not take Greenspan's remarks as an indication of an imminent tightening of monetary policy.
"I felt that he said ... monetary policy is not going to change in the short-run," said Jonathan Francis, head of global strategy at Putnam Investments.
The Fed last changed rates in January 1996, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent.
Francis said he felt Greenspan's remarks indicated workers are feeling more secure about their employment situation, but that is not yet a reason to justify a rate hike.

"People are being more active now leaving one job and looking for another one. So in that sense I would characterize us as being one step closer to the end of this transitional process, but not yet there," Francis said.
"So my assessment is that at least (based) on the data that they (Fed officials) have in hand today, there will be no change in monetary policy," Francis said.
Experts also said the strength of the U.S. dollar after Greenspan's speech hinted foreign investors do not appear to be ready to bail out of the U.S. Treasury market yet.

"From a foreign investor's point of view you do have a dollar that is more likely to rise than fall and as a consequence with higher yields and a strong currnecy, it still represents a fairly attractive market for foreign investors," Putnam's Francis said.

Foreigners have been seen by many in the market as active Treasury buyers for quite some time now. Some analysts even said that continued foreign interest could offset any possible major domestic selling of government debt securities.
A few experts, however, dropped a word of caution on the outlook for the U.S. Treasury yield curve.
Merrill Lynch's fixed-income strategist Thomas Sowanick said he expects the U.S. yield curve to flatten sharply over the next six months.
He added that the spread between the two-year note and the 30-year bond might adopt a flat posture or even become slightly inverted over the next two quarters.
"I think ... we could have a pretty sharp flattening of the yield curve," Sowanick said.
